title: GitHub Copilot vs Cursor for Writing Test Code: Six Months of Daily Use
excerpt: After six months of using both GitHub Copilot and Cursor on real QA projects — writing Playwright, pytest, and API test suites — here is an honest breakdown of where each tool actually helps and where it quietly wastes your time.
content:
Six months ago I set a personal rule: every test I write goes through an AI assistant first. No exceptions. The goal was to force myself to actually stress-test these tools rather than cherry-pick the impressive demos. I have been running Cursor and GitHub Copilot side-by-side across three projects — a React SPA with a Playwright E2E suite, a FastAPI backend covered by pytest, and a Node.js microservice with Vitest — and what I found surprised me in both directions.

The short version: neither tool is clearly better. Each one has a distinct personality, and matching that personality to your workflow matters more than the raw benchmark numbers you will find in vendor whitepapers.

## How They Actually Behave When You Are Writing Tests

![](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1516116216624-53e697fedbea?w=800&q=80)


Copilot, now part of GitHub's broader AI ecosystem with significant capability expansions through 2024–2025, is a ghost in your editor. It watches what you type and offers completions. When I am writing a pytest fixture, it is genuinely good at inferring the shape of the next test from the ones above it. If I have already written three tests for a `UserService` class with a consistent `# Arrange / # Act / # Assert` structure, Copilot picks up that pattern almost immediately and carries it forward. For repetitive test authoring — think data-driven tests over a REST API's validation rules — it is fast and accurate enough that I have stopped caring about how it works internally.

The problem is depth. Copilot lives at the line or block level. It does not understand your entire test suite architecture. If your `conftest.py` has fifteen fixtures with non-obvious interdependencies, Copilot does not know about them unless you are actively editing those files. I have wasted more time than I care to admit chasing down a generated test that used a fixture name that *almost* matched one of mine — different module, wrong scope. The autocomplete was confident; the test was wrong.

Cursor is fundamentally different in its model. It gives you a chat interface (Cmd+L) and an Agent mode that can read, write, and edit multiple files simultaneously. The Composer — what Cursor calls its multi-file editing mode — is what sets it apart for QA work. When I described a new endpoint I wanted to cover and asked Cursor to generate tests, it opened my existing test file, read the fixture definitions from `conftest.py`, checked the models in `schemas.py`, and wrote tests that actually used my project's real fixtures instead of inventing new ones. That is a qualitatively different experience from anything Copilot offers today.

Cursor crossed $500M ARR and a $10B valuation in 2025, which tells you the market has noticed this difference too. The 0.50 release introduced Background Agents — autonomous processes that can run tests, read failure output, and propose fixes without you staying in the loop. I have used it to run a failing Playwright suite and have Cursor diagnose the selector drift on its own. It gets it right about 60% of the time, which sounds underwhelming until you realize the alternative is you doing that triage manually.

## Where Copilot Still Wins

I want to be fair here because I see a lot of hot takes that dismiss Copilot as obsolete. For certain workflows, it is still the better tool.

First, inline speed. Cursor's chat and agent interactions require context-switching. You are opening a panel, describing what you want, reviewing a diff. For a senior engineer who knows exactly what they need to write, Copilot's ghost text is faster for straightforward completions. When I am in a flow state writing Vitest unit tests for utility functions, I do not want a chat window — I want the next `it()` block suggested before I finish typing the description.

Second, IDE integration breadth. Copilot works in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ, WebStorm, PyCharm), Neovim, and more. Cursor is a VS Code fork. If your team is on WebStorm for a Java backend with JUnit 5, Copilot is your only real AI-native option right now. I hit this exactly when a colleague asked me to help generate tests for a Spring Boot service — Cursor simply was not on the table.

Third, trust in enterprise environments. GitHub Copilot Business and Enterprise give administrators usage APIs, org-level custom instructions stored in `.github` repos, and proper audit trails. Starting in late 2025, org-wide Copilot instructions can be version-controlled in a `.github` repo — a feature that makes rollout, auditing, and rollback of AI configuration genuinely manageable. Cursor has improved on this front, but GitHub's compliance story is more mature. For QA engineers at companies with strict data governance, that matters.

Lastly, test quality research is encouraging. A 2024 ACM/IEEE study on Copilot for Python test generation found it produced syntactically valid code at a 91.5% rate. In my own use, Copilot's generated assertions are usually correct in structure — the `assert response.status_code == 200` patterns are solid. Where it falls apart is semantic correctness: it does not know your business logic, and it will write a test that passes but does not actually cover the case you care about.

## Where Cursor Pulls Ahead for Real QA Work

![](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1542831371-29b0f74f9713?w=800&q=80)


The honest gap between these tools opens up the moment you move beyond single-function unit tests.

For E2E test generation in Playwright, Cursor's multi-file context is the difference between a useful suggestion and a production-ready test. When I asked Cursor to write a test for a multi-step checkout flow, I gave it the page object files, the existing fixtures, and a brief description of the flow. It generated a test that correctly imported the `CheckoutPage` and `CartPage` objects, used the existing `authenticatedPage` fixture, and structured the assertions consistently with the rest of the suite. Getting equivalent output from Copilot required me to have the right files open in adjacent tabs and manually coax the completions, which felt like writing the test twice.

For debugging failing tests, Cursor is in a different league. I run the test, copy the failure output into the chat, and ask what is wrong. Because Cursor already has the context of the test file and relevant source files, it can often pinpoint whether the issue is a changed selector, a misaligned fixture expectation, or an actual application regression. Copilot has no equivalent workflow — it is a completion tool, not a diagnostic one.

CI integration is another area where the difference is stark. I had Cursor read a GitHub Actions workflow YAML, identify why a Playwright test step was timing out (the `--workers` flag was not being passed, so tests were running serially), and write the corrected YAML. It took about forty seconds. That kind of cross-file, cross-concern reasoning is where Cursor's architecture shines.

One important caveat: Cursor's agent mode suggestions are not always correct, and the confidence with which it presents wrong answers is a legitimate hazard. I had it regenerate a `pytest-asyncio` fixture incorrectly twice in the same session because it was not accounting for the `asyncio_mode = auto` setting in `pyproject.toml`. It found the error on the third prompt when I explicitly told it to check the config file. The lesson: treat Cursor's agent output the same way you would treat code from a smart junior engineer — review it, do not just approve it.

## The Real Cost Question

Pricing shapes real adoption decisions. GitHub Copilot Individual runs at $10/month; Copilot Business is $19/user/month. Cursor Pro is $20/month, with a Business tier at $40/user/month as of 2025.

For a solo QA engineer, both are defensible at those prices if they save even thirty minutes a day. The math is easy. For teams, the question is whether Cursor's more powerful context engine justifies double the Copilot Business price. My answer: if your team is writing mostly unit and integration tests and already has strong conventions the AI can mimic, Copilot is sufficient and cheaper. If you are maintaining large E2E suites with complex fixture hierarchies, or you are frequently onboarding new tests into a legacy codebase, Cursor's Agent mode pays for itself.

## What I Actually Use Today

After six months I have not picked one tool and dropped the other. I use Copilot in VS Code for unit test authoring sessions where I am in flow and want fast inline completions. I switch to Cursor when I am doing anything that requires understanding the broader test architecture: adding a new page object model, debugging a flaky Playwright test, or generating test coverage for a new feature across multiple layers.

That dual-tool approach is slightly annoying, but it reflects where AI-assisted testing genuinely is right now. Copilot is a very fast autocomplete with decent test pattern awareness. Cursor is a junior QA engineer who can read your whole codebase but occasionally hallucinates fixture names.

The version to watch is whatever ships in both tools over the next six months. Copilot's rollout of MCP OAuth support and file-based org instructions signals it is moving toward deeper project context. Cursor's Background Agents are getting more reliable with each release. The gap between them is real today — I would bet it is narrower by mid-2026.

For now: if you are only going to use one, audit what kind of tests dominate your day-to-day work. That answer will tell you which tool to buy.
